books.section: Topic 3.12 Movement in the Early Republic

primary_sources: George Caleb Bingham, Daniel Boone Escorting Settlers through the Cumberland Gap, 1851-52

stimulus.text: George Caleb Bingham, Daniel Boone Escorting Settlers through the Cumberland Gap, 1851–52. The painting shows a man in buckskin carrying a rifle, leading a white horse with a woman rider, followed by armed settlers and a dog, through a rocky mountain pass. Background from the books: Daniel Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap in 1775, opening a path for settlers into Kentucky.
stimulus.source_note: George Caleb Bingham, Daniel Boone Escorting Settlers through the Cumberland Gap, 1851-52, oil on canvas, Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, Washington University in St. Louis. Public domain. Image viewed before writing.

options.text: A battle between settlers and British soldiers in Kentucky.
options.misconception: No battle is shown; the settlers walk in a line through a pass.

options.text: A town meeting voting on Kentucky statehood.
options.misconception: No meeting or vote appears in the painting.

options.text: A surveyor marking out townships north of the Ohio River.
options.misconception: No survey lines or instruments appear; the scene is a mountain pass.

options.text: Daniel Boone leading a line of settlers through the Cumberland Gap.

rationales.A: The settlers walk forward in a line; no one is fighting.
rationales.B: The painting shows a journey, not a meeting or a vote.
rationales.C: The scene is a rocky pass, not a survey of townships.
rationales.D: Boone in buckskin leads the line, with settlers and a woman on a white horse behind him, through a mountain pass.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the front of the line: a man in buckskin leads.
2. Behind him walk settlers, and a woman rides a white horse.
3. The group moves through a narrow pass between cliffs.
4. So the painting shows Boone guiding settlers through the Cumberland Gap toward Kentucky.
Remember: in a painting, follow the line of people to find the action.
